# Inclusion Probabilities

## Definitions

1. **First-order** inclusion probability:
$$ \pi_i=\text{Prob}(i\in s)=\sum\limits_{S;\ i \in s} p(s)$$
2. **Second-order** inclusion probability:
$$ \pi_{ij}=\text{Prob}(i, j \in s)=\sum\limits_{S;\ i,j \in s} p(s)$$
3. Random sampling design: $\pi_i>0, \ \ \forall i \in U$
4. Measurable sampling design: $\pi_{ij}>0, \ \ \forall i,j \in U$

## Definitions

- $I_i$: indicator variable of membership in the sample ($s$)
$$
  I_i =
    \begin{cases}
      1 & \text{if } i \in s\\
      0 & \text{otherwise}
    \end{cases}
$$

Keep in mind:

- $E(I_i)=\pi_i$
- $E(I_iI_j)=\pi_{ij}$
- $V(I_i)=\pi_i(1-\pi_i)$
- $Cov(I_i,I_j)=\pi_{ij}-\pi_i\pi_j=\Delta_{ij}$

- $n_s=\sum\nolimits_{i\in U} I_i$: is the (expected) sample size. If $n_s$ does not depend on the sample $s$, then it is fixed and $V(n_s)=0$.

## Example: simple random sampling

- **Idea:** choose $n$ individuals out of $N$ **without replacement**.
    1. Every sample of size $n$ has the same probability of being selected.
    2. There are $C_n^N$ distinct samples of size $n$.

::: {.block}
::: {.block-title}
Definition
:::
Simple random design:
$$
  p(s) =
    \begin{cases}
      1/C_n^N & \text{if the sample is of size } n\\
      0 & \text{otherwise}
    \end{cases}
$$
:::

## Example: simple random sampling

Under SRS, the inclusion probabilities are:

$$\pi_i=n/N$$

$$\pi_{ij}=\frac{n(n-1)}{N(N-1)} \quad \forall \ i \neq j$$

## Properties of the inclusion probabilities

1. $\pi_{ii}=\pi_i$ and $\pi_{ij}=\pi_{ji}$
2. For a design with (expected) sample size:
$$\sum\limits_{i\in U} \pi_i=n $$
3. For a fixed-size sampling design ($n_s=n$):
$$\sum\limits_{i\in U} \pi_{ij}=n\pi_j$$
and for $\Delta_{ij}=\pi_{ij} - \pi_i\pi_j$,
$$ \sum\limits_{j\in U} \Delta_{ij}=0$$

# The HT Estimator

## Horvitz–Thompson ($\pi$) estimator

::: {.block}
::: {.block-title}
Definition
:::
The Horvitz–Thompson (HT) estimator of the total of variable $y$, $Y=\sum\nolimits_{i\in U}y_i$, is:
$$\hat Y_{\text{HT}}=\sum\limits_{i\in s} \frac{y_i}{\pi_i}=\sum\limits_{i\in s} w_i\times y_i $$
where $w_i=1/\pi_i$ is called the weight of individual $i$.
:::

- Remark: the HT estimator only exists for random samples.

## Properties of the HT estimator

::: {.block}
::: {.block-title}
Unbiased
:::
$$E(\hat Y_{\text{HT}})=Y $$
:::

::: {.block}
::: {.block-title}
Variance
:::
$$V(\hat Y_{\text{HT}})=\sum\limits_{i\in U}\sum\limits_{j\in U} (\pi_{ij}-\pi_i\pi_j)\frac{y_i}{\pi_i}\frac{y_j}{\pi_j} $$
:::

## Properties of the HT estimator

If the sample size is fixed (i.e. $V(n_s)=0$):

$$V(\hat Y_{\text{HT}})=-\frac{1}{2}\sum\limits_{i\in U}\sum\limits_{j\in U}(\pi_{ij}-\pi_i\pi_j) \left[\frac{y_i}{\pi_i}-\frac{y_j}{\pi_j}\right]^2 $$

This equation is called Sen–Yates–Grundy (SYG).

## Example

Consider the following sampling design for the finite population $U=\{1,2,3\}$:

| sample ($s$) | $p(s)$ | HT estimator |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| $s_1=\{1,2\}$ | 0.5  | |
| $s_2=\{1,3\}$ | 0.25 | |
| $s_3=\{2,3\}$ | 0.25 | |

1. Compute the first-order inclusion probabilities for each individual of the population.
2. Compute the HT estimator for each sample.
3. Verify that the HT estimator is unbiased.

# Variance Estimation

## Variance estimation

- Unbiased variance estimator: we want to find a statistic $\hat V$ such that $E(\hat V)=\text{Var}(\hat Y_{\text{HT}})$.
- **Idea:** if $\pi_{ij}>0\ \forall i,j \in U$, we can apply the "principle" of the HT estimator:

$$\hat V(\hat Y_{\text{HT}})=\sum\limits_{i\in s}\sum\limits_{j\in s} \frac{(\pi_{ij}-\pi_i\pi_j)}{\pi_{ij}}\frac{y_i}{\pi_i}\frac{y_j}{\pi_j} $$

If the sample size is fixed (i.e. $V(n_s)=0$):

$$\hat V(\hat Y_{\text{HT}})=-\frac{1}{2}\sum\limits_{i\in s}\sum\limits_{j\in s}\frac{(\pi_{ij}-\pi_i\pi_j)}{\pi_{ij}} \left[\frac{y_i}{\pi_i}-\frac{y_j}{\pi_j}\right]^2 $$

## Example

Consider the following sampling design for the finite population $U=\{1,2,3\}$ with $y_1=16$, $y_2=21$ and $y_3=18$:

| sample ($s$) | $p(s)$ | HT estimate | HT var estimate |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| $s_1=\{1,2\}$ | 0.5  | | |
| $s_2=\{1,3\}$ | 0.25 | | |
| $s_3=\{2,3\}$ | 0.25 | | |

Verify that the variance estimator is unbiased.
